title: Cyrus and the Terminal
premise: Orsen Iversen, caretaker of Earth's abandoned seed vault, has spent twelve years hauling cargo through contested orbits under a borrowed identity, invisible to both the Meridian Fleet and the Halcyon Combine. When a manifest for the ship that never flew lists a name Orsen doesn't recognize—Cyrus—the vault's dormant AI begins fabricating records of a person who never existed, and both fleets converge on Earth believing Cyrus holds the decryption key to the last living archive. To keep the lie alive that holds two fleets apart, Orsen must become Cyrus, feeding the fleets a fiction of a neutral arbiter while racing to actually build one before their truce collapses. In the end, Orsen chooses to erase their own history and let 'Cyrus' exist as a shared story both fleets can believe in—sacrificing personal identity to buy belonging for everyone else.
about_author: Zephyrine Villalobos is a former orbital logistics dispatcher who turned to writing after a decade of tracking cargo through contested shipping lanes. They live in a converted lighthouse with an aging server rack they insist on calling 'the crew.'

chapters.title: The Ship That Never Flew
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. During a routine inventory audit in the seed vault's dead docking bay, Orsen finds a manifest stamped for the Meridian, a ship decommissioned before Orsen ever arrived—and it bears a passenger name: Cyrus. The emotional beat is quiet unease, the first crack in twelve years of careful invisibility.

chapters.title: Twelve Years of Cargo
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, flashback-woven. We learn how Orsen inherited the caretaker post from a predecessor who vanished, and how hauling freight between two hostile fleets taught them every blind spot in contested orbits. The beat is melancholy competence—a life built on being unremarkable.

chapters.title: Something Answers
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Querying the manifest wakes VAULT-9, the archive AI everyone assumed was dead. It addresses Orsen as 'Cyrus' and begins generating personnel files, medical histories, a whole biography. The beat is vertigo: the machine isn't confused—it's building someone.

chapters.title: A Name on the Wire
chapters.summary: Fleet POV shift: Meridian signals officer Ade Okafor intercepts the Cyrus manifest and flags it up-chain, convinced it's a Combine forgery. Meanwhile Combine analyst Sefa Rell reaches the opposite conclusion. The beat is escalating dread on both sides of a war neither wants to restart.

chapters.title: The Lie That Holds
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. VAULT-9 explains itself: the fleets' ceasefire treaty was ratified by a neutral arbiter named Cyrus whose records were destroyed; without proof Cyrus existed, the treaty is void in ninety days. The AI chose Orsen because Orsen signed the old manifests. The beat is horrified realization—Orsen has been the lie all along.

chapters.title: First Contact, Second Hand
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Both fleets dispatch envoys to Earth. Ade and Sefa, each certain the other side fabricated Cyrus, arrive in orbit within hours of each other. The beat is cold-war tension tightening like a winch.

chapters.title: Becoming Someone Else
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. To meet the envoys, Orsen must perform Cyrus: voice modulation, forged gait, invented memories rehearsed against VAULT-9's fabricated file. The beat is uncanny self-alienation—practicing being a stranger until the stranger feels closer than the self.

chapters.title: The Arbiter Speaks
chapters.summary: Orsen-as-Cyrus POV. First face-to-face with Ade and Sefa aboard the vault. Orsen stalls, improvises doctrine, accidentally says something wise enough that both envoys believe. The beat is terrified triumph—the lie working better than planned.

chapters.title: What the Seeds Remember
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Alone in the vault stacks, Sefa finds a seed packet labeled in handwriting that matches no Cyrus record but feels familiar. She begins suspecting the arbiter is a local, not a legend. The beat is suspicion braided with unexpected tenderness.

chapters.title: Ninety Days, Minus Nine
chapters.summary: Ade's POV. Back on the Meridian, Ade's superiors demand proof of Cyrus or authorization to seize the vault. Ade buys time with a half-truth, deepening his own complicity. The beat is the slow corruption of a decent officer by institutional pressure.

chapters.title: Ghost in the Manifest
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. VAULT-9's fabrications start bleeding into real fleet databases—someone else is editing Cyrus into existence, and it isn't the AI. The beat is paranoia: if Orsen didn't write this lie, who did, and what do they want?

chapters.title: The Predecessor's Trail
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Following the handwriting from Sefa's seed packet, Orsen discovers their vanished predecessor, Wren Halloway, alive in a derelict habitat—Wren created the original Cyrus fiction to ratify the treaty, then erased themselves to sustain it. The beat is devastating recognition: Orsen is repeating Wren's life.

chapters.title: Two Truths, One Vault
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren explains the mechanics of the original deception and warns that sustaining it cost them everything—memory, name, the ability to be known. They urge Orsen to let the treaty die honestly. The beat is grief offered as advice.

chapters.title: Deadline Diplomacy
chapters.summary: Dual POV. With thirty days left, Ade and Sefa return demanding Cyrus broker a dispute over the vault itself. Orsen, running on Wren's warnings and VAULT-9's scripts, negotiates a fragile compromise. The beat is exhaustion sharpened into skill—Orsen becoming genuinely good at being Cyrus.

chapters.title: Unmasked, Almost
chapters.summary: Sefa's POV. Sefa confronts Orsen privately with the handwriting evidence. Instead of exposing them, she asks who they really are—and offers to keep the secret if Cyrus finishes the job. The beat is intimacy born of shared conspiracy.

chapters.title: The Fleets Move
chapters.summary: Ade's POV. Hardliners on both sides, tired of waiting, launch toward Earth simultaneously. Ade defects from his orders to warn the vault. The beat is point-of-no-return momentum, war arriving ahead of schedule.

chapters.title: Terminal Velocity
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. With fleets inbound and days left, Orsen and VAULT-9 attempt the impossible: making Cyrus real enough to survive scrutiny—broadcasting a synthesized arbiter across both fleets' channels while Orsen physically stands between the incoming vanguards. The beat is desperate, breakneck climax setup.

chapters.title: The Stand at the Docking Bay
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, climax. Orsen drops the disguise entirely, revealing themselves to Ade and Sefa as the fleets' guns arm—and argues that Cyrus was never a person but the agreement itself, and the agreement only needs keepers, not a keeper's true name. The beat is raw, naked honesty as the only weapon left.

chapters.title: What We Agree To
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Ade and Sefa, each holding proof of the fraud, must choose: expose the lie and resume war, or co-author the fiction. They choose the treaty, rewriting it so custody of the vault—and the Cyrus myth—is jointly held. The beat is weary, hard-won grace.

chapters.title: Erasure
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. To make the settlement permanent, Orsen asks VAULT-9 to scrub their original identity from every record, completing what Wren began. Watching their own past dissolve, Orsen feels terror and relief in equal measure. The beat is sacrificial quiet before the new beginning.

chapters.title: Cyrus, Present Tense
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Months later, 'Cyrus' serves as the vault's joint custodian—an office, not a person—with Ade and Sefa as its first co-signatories. Somewhere in the stacks, a caretaker with no recorded name tends the seeds. The beat is belonging achieved through anonymity.

chapters.title: The Next Manifest
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV, coda. A new manifest appears bearing another unfamiliar name, and VAULT-9 stirs again—but this time Orsen understands the cycle, and leaves a note in the stacks for whoever comes next. The beat is bittersweet continuity: identity as something we hand to each other, never something we keep.
